The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Guilbault (Saint-Jacques):
That this House regrets that, after less than three months in office, the Government is in growing disarray as demonstrated by its harmful, inadequately considered and irresponsible cuts in government services of importance to the economic and social development of the regions and of individual Canadians as well as by Ministers' apparent inability to manage their departments and their relations with the provinces and with the public.

Since the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) was in the middle of his question and comment period, I will advise the House that there are eight minutes remaining for questions and comments.
If there are no questions or comments, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Kootenay West.

Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to wonder if today was in fact an Opposition day. I was also beginning to wonder if the Opposition was serious about the Opposition day. 1 thought that the Opposition might proceed in the next hour to deal with Questions on the Order Paper and to filibuster the House. That would give us an indication of how serious it is not about the embarrassing motion which has been proposed. The motion is embarrassing to the Opposition.
It is your Government that is embarrassing.

Let me review the Opposition motion. It states that the Government is in growing disarray "as demonstrated by its harmful, inadequately considered and irresponsible cuts". Including the words "inadequately considered" would infer that we really have not examined the matter in any depth and that what we should do is resort to greater study. For the record, Mr. Speaker, I would like to turn to Hansard of November 7, 1984, at page 38. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said, and I quote:
Studies are not action. Process is not an agenda for progress. The Prime Minister and his Party have a massive majority.
At least we can agree on that.
We can see it in this House. We can see it all around us. Now they are the Government. Now they must face the tough issues and difficult decisions.
That is what the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition asked us to do, that is what we are doing and that is what that Party
December 3, 1984

is now complaining about. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition goes on to say, and I quote:
That is what their role is. That is what the Canadian poeple put them into office to do, not to study, contemplate, ruminate and meditate.
What do we find today, Mr. Speaker? We find an article in The Citizen entitled "Sky High", and the relationship to the title is the $1 million cost of the probe into the crash of Air Canada's Gimli Glider. I think it should more likely be called the "Gimli gimmick" which was perpetrated on the Canadian people by the former Minister of Transport. The former Minister of Transport insisted that the probe be held in Winnipeg, coincidentally in his riding, because, after all, Gimli is not too far away from Winnipeg and that is where the Air Canada Boeing 767 went down, out of gas. Therefore, it should follow that that is where the study should be held. But how many times did that commission manage to get to Gimli? Just once, Mr. Speaker. Yet that commission managed to go to Vancouver, London, Frankfurt, Zurich, Paris, Seattle, San Francisco, Manhattan, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Montreal and Edmonton in order to find out how an airplane runs out of gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And it never ran out of gas once.

You are right. And the study is still not ready. That is the kind of contemplation and rumination which the former government indulged in. Those Hon. Members should not ask us to perform that kind of self-examination of our navels at an enormous cost to the taxpayers.
The Liberal Party says that the cuts in government services, which are of importance to the economic and social development of the regions, is irresponsible. The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) said this morning: "We must be putting more money into people's pockets". What that means in effect is that we do not cut, we spend. If that is not what the Hon. Member is saying, then I stand to be corrected. What I believe he is saying is that we do not decrease the deficit, we increase it.
The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor advised us that he is an economist. As such he is some form of a specialist. I must say, however, that that specialty is in deep trouble in his Party. Mr. Laxer tells us that he is in deep trouble in terms of his Party because the Party is in deep trouble in terms of its economic philosophy. I recall on Cross Country Checkup when the Leader of the New Democratic Party was waxing eloquently about how up to date his Party was in its philosophy and policy. He was really upset with Mr. Laxer and was letting Canadians know that the New Democratic Party was right on its economic track. When was the program Cross Country Checkup aired? It was just before the election campaign. It was in 1984 and the closest year the Leader of the New Democratic Party could refer to as reference was 1979. He said his Party went along with the Liberals in 1979, but he is right out of touch in 1984. I do not believe he has ever read Orwell. If he has, he must have started at the back of the book and read it in reverse. The corollary is that we do not discourage investment, we encourage it, thereby encouraging
Supply
Canadians to put their savings into the elements which are going to bring this country back from the brink of disaster and rebuild the economy.
I would be very interested in terms of the election campaign just past to know what the Liberal policy is on this particular problem with which we are faced, the deficit. How does the Liberal Party rationalize its motion? I would like to know what the New Democratic Party policy is. I say that on the basis of my experience in appearing on eight or ten open line shows during the period of the election campaign.
What a spectacle, Mr. Speaker, of the Liberal candidate looking through her policy book-which consisted of three pages, handwritten. Finally, in the last week of the election campaign, glory be, there it was with the Liberal logo on the front. It was official. When I asked the former Hon. Member for Kootenay West what his Party's policy on mining was, he did not know. He did not believe there was a policy on mining.
I knew what the New Democratic Party's policy on forestry was because it had copied ours. That was a great help because at least we could communicate on that subject. There are two main resources of Kootenay West, mining and forestry, and at least the former Hon. Member for Kootenay West was half right; but there was an absence of policy as indicated by the thinness of the manual. It looked like a starved child.
During the election campaign I had the opportunity, as did many Canadians, to listen to the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor speak on the CBC in programs of national consequence. In fairness, I wondered what that Party had to offer us. If they could not tell us what the answers were, at least they could give us some concrete solutions or suggestions. That is what I had hoped for, and some things which the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor had to say did make sense.
However, this House of Commons is the place not just for debate; it is a place where one should be prepared to listen to the concrete solutions of either the Government or the Opposition. Just because one is in opposition is no justification to slam and kick. It is an opportunity to offer alternatives. But I have yet to hear from Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party or Hon. Members of the Liberal Party as to any alternatives. I have heard them say "Cut this, butcher that, do this", but in terms of laying out in a sensible and cohesive manner a proposal which any Party could consider, be they on this side or the other side, I would have to say how disappointed I am in the rabble across the way.
The motion moved by the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), Mr. Speaker, refers to "harmful, inadequately considered and irresponsible cuts". Let me ask Hon. Members opposite where they were when the NDP got together with the Liberals on the National Energy Program, a total economic disaster? Were they ever in Alberta or northern British Columbia, or were they comfortably sequestered in their seats in this House of Commons? Did you see any of these Hon. Members out in northern British Columbia, off the beaten track in the Fort St. John gas-producing area? Did you

December 3, 1984
Supply
see them at drill sites in Alberta? No, sir! I can remember reading a document in which the NDP energy critic thought that tar sands and heavy oil were the same thing. So much for knowledge. So much for the ability to criticize intelligently.
How many Members opposite realize that when you drill for oil it is not just a brace and bit. When you drill for oil you are talking about a structure that takes two years to build and costs millions of dollars. It requires up to 40 flatbed trucks to move it from one site to another. In the case of a deep well, it is 64 trucks. But they do not realize that, Mr. Speaker. They did not see the industry shut down, the trucks parked and unmoving. Neither did they see the tool retrieval firms with half a dozen employees go bankrupt. They did not see the suppliers of equipment and services to the oil and gas sector. How many of them ever went to the small town of Drayton Valley and looked at the number of houses for sale? None of them, Mr. Speaker. They were in isolation, wrapped up in their House of Commons cocoons. They dared not step off the threshold.
The bottom line is that they have never cared for the West. Never! The Party with its roots in the West is the very Party that abrogated its responsibility to the West. I speak of the NDP. That, Mr. Speaker, is what has brought about their demise and will continue to do so.
They pose questions about economic and social development of the regions. We have had some howling about the four and a half person-years being removed from the interpretation centre at the Creston Valley Wildlife Management area. I have not heard a word out of these people opposite about the social and economic impact on loggers, truckers and other equipment operators of the rebate of 20 cents a gallon on fuel taxes for the resource sector. I have not heard a word about the difference that is going to make to the trucker who has to haul logs some 40 miles over back roads. I have not heard a word about the fact that this 20-cent rebate will mean that, on the basis of fuel consumption and mileage, a trucker will now be able to buy one new tire a month, and there are 18 tires on a logging truck. I have not heard a word about the fact that that rebate can mean the difference between survival and failure, between employment and unemployment, in the fragile forest industry of British Columbia. I have not heard a word about the opportunities provided to the mining sector. But then of course, they really have not asked about them, Mr. Speaker.
The motion, as framed, is specious and frivolous, particularly when I hear them talk about the social consequences. Do not talk to me about social consequences when I represent a riding with the highest unemployment rate in British Columbia at 24 per cent.
What are you doing about it?
Working a darn sight harder on it in this House of Commons than you are, sir.
Answer the question.
I would be pleased to answer your question after 1 have had my shot.
Answer it right now.

No, I am not going to bother with your frivolous question at this moment.
When it comes to the social and economic consequences of 24 per cent unemployment, I have seen them. Why do you suppose that the third floor of the Nelson Hospital has 12 beds occupied now instead of one? Why do you suppose the people occupying those beds are there by virtue of acute mental and psychological depression? It is because in Nelson, B.C., there is a 24 per cent unemployment rate.
In Kootenay West we have the highest unemployment rate in British Columbia, and among the eight highest in Canada. When they talk to me about social consequences, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that those miners are glad to have the opportunity to get back to work. Forest workers, loggers, truck drivers, skidders, they are all delighted at the opportunity to know that this 20-cent rebate, taken across the board, can mean the difference between survival and failure. But what do I see here? I see a member of the Liberal Party grinning. I hope he never has the misfortune to have the level of unemployment in his constituency that I have in mine. If he did, he would not be sitting there grinning. He would understand the impact that has on the people I care for and whom he should be caring for.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I will turn to a statement by the Economic Council of Canada. They have again reminded us of how we got into our current fiscal mess. Perhaps the Liberals and NDP on the opposite side who have a grain of doubt in their minds should carve this in stone on their foreheads. What happened was quite simple, and I quote:
We designed elaborate government programs in the sixties, and added to them in the seventies. Yet the economic growth to pay for the programs faded in the seventies, opening an increasing gap between expenditures and revenues. The recession of 1981-82 blew the gap wide open, sending the federal deficit from $ 10-billion to $35-billion.
They went on to say:
Tighter spending controls, a review of some 'tax expenditures' and a more relaxed monetary policy is the combination the country requires.
Those are the proposals put forward by the Economic Council of Canada. I look forward to listening to some good sense and good suggestions from the opposition side. How refreshing that would be in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to my hon. friend that despite the differences in this House, no one grins about unemployment, whether it is in his riding, mine, in eastern Canada or western Canada.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member about the unemployment situation in his own riding. The Hon. Member's Government was elected on a promise of job creation as the first priority, not necessarily cutting the deficit. His Leader and caucus went around the country from east to west promising thousands of jobs overnight. I would think they were also referring to the Hon. Member's riding. What does the Hon.
December 3, 1984

Member's Government have to propose concerning job creation for the people in his riding and others? Give us some solutions instead of only talking about concepts and the idea of co-operation, consideration and consultation. Many Canadians believe that such talk adds up only to vegetation. Let the Hon. Member tell us what he proposes not only for his riding but for other ridings across this country that face unemployment. Let him put those proposals on the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I have no difficulty in responding to that question in terms of my own riding. I would rather not offer solutions for all the other ridings because that is a rather heavy responsibility to deal with today. However, I am more than prepared to respond in terms of the constituency of Kootenay West.
What has the Government done? If the Hon. Member had been paying attention he would have heard that the forestry sector in British Columbia is in very serious trouble. It is facing oversupply primarily as a result of cutting wood for nothing else but two by fours. The economy has forced that sector to consider modernization, expansion and efficiency. We have provided the ways and means for such improvements to one sawmill in particular through assistance in the sum of approximately $1.25 million, which will guarantee the maintenance of existing jobs. In terms of the Hon. Member's question, I believe that is an example of what the Government is doing.
We are also considering an application by Cominco-which is the largest silver, lead and zinc producer in the free world- for assistance in the construction of a new lead smelter in Trail. That will generate 600 jobs directly for six years. The spin-off benefits in the ratio of two to one should be evident to the Hon. Member. The application of that particular project would certainly prevent a directly negative impact on approximately 3,000 jobs along with the spin-off effect on 40,000 people living in a number of communities.
I would suggest that the initiative, which has been approved, and the Cominco application, which is being studied, will go a long way to help to secure job opportunities and create additional job opportunities in the forestry sector.
I have already mentioned the impact of the 20 cent per gallon tax abatement on diesel and gasoline fuels for off-road use in the bush and in the mining sector.

Mr. Speaker, I am goaded into making some comments and asking a brief question. First, I would suggest that if the Hon. Member read Hansard more carefully, he would see that there are four occasions since this session started when, as our Party's spokesman for economic development, I laid out positive suggestions for reviving the economy.
I have made speeches about industrial development, agricultural policy, tax policy and trade strategy. If the Hon. Member is interested, I can give him the references.
He also suggested that there was a comment in my criticism of the Government dealing with putting money in people's
Supply
pockets and that somehow it suggested irresponsibility. I was suggesting, and continue to stress, that it is crucial to our economy to put more money into the pockets of the taxpayers of this country who, I believe, are overtaxed. The economic crisis in this country, as in fact analysed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), stressed the problem of consumer confidence. His approach to creating more confidence has been tax those people more and to cut back public sector services.
It is our opinion that such an approach does not make sense since one creates more consumer confidence by allowing ordinary Canadians to have more money in order to be able to spend more and have a greater sense of security for the future.
How can the Hon. Member, as a Conservative, stand up in the House and make the kind of commentary he does when so many of his colleagues in the last Parliament made commitments, such as to ensure that borrowing does not take place for the next fiscal year, to provide, an open government, and to consult with groups affected by policies, yet his own Government is taking a step by step move away from those past commitments?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). If he cares to provide me with the page reference to his comments on agriculture, the tax system and economic development, I would be pleased to read them.
In his remarks this morning, the Hon. Member made frequent reference to butchery when I hoped that he would give some solid and forthright suggestions about what his Party's policy would be as a solution.
He stated that there is too much taxation and that taxpayers should have more money in their pockets. However, the economic indicators suggest that there should be more taxation. The Economic Council of Canada is saying that there should be more taxation. It also stated that any government is fearful of adding to the tax burden of taxpayers.
If I understood the Hon. Member correctly, when he spoke of putting money into people's pockets, he meant reverting back to the grant system. While there are times when I believe the grant system is more appropriate, I have seen some major abuses of the grant system in my constituency. When the Canada Works applications come before my advisory board, they will be most carefully screened. I do not want to see an apple juicing plant erected in a community where there are no apple trees. I do not want someone given a grant to build a pelton wheel factory, only to have that building revert to that person for him to sell when in fact no pelton wheels are produced. It is that kind of use of the grant system that I am against.
With respect to the issue of seeking borrowing authority for the next fiscal year, I think the Hon. Member must realize that, for the Government to implement even to a degree only the programs which his own Party espouses as well as our programs that will help generate short-term employment and meaningful long-term job training, borrowing is necessary at this stage. I do not like it any more than the Hon. Member,

December 3, 1984
Supply
but it is an issue that has confronted us and one which we have acted upon. We must bite the bullet, and we have done so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now over. We will resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to enter the debate on the opposition motion of the Liberal Party. Basically, the motion states that after less than three months the Government does not seem to know where it is going.
While I support the motion, having sat in the House the last number of years when the Liberals were in power, I have often wondered whether the Liberal government knew where it was going. In most instances the Liberal government did not know where it was going. It was crisis management, going from pillar to post and not really providing any leadership for Canadians and for our economy.
The September 4 election of the new Government, I hasten to add, brought with it a lot of promise and hope, but we have seen in the last three months what type of direction this Government wants to take. To tell you the truth, Mr. Speaker, I am quite afraid. At first 1 was quite hopeful. While in Opposition I had an opportunity to talk and meet with a fair number of members of the Conservative Party. I got the impression that many were people with whom I could associate myself. Many were small "c" Conservatives who were concerned about preserving and conserving.
I am very committed to the notion of a conserving society. I believe that Canada and most of the industrialized western countries are going through major economic, social and environmental changes. The rapid growth in the past has in many ways reached its limits. For society to survive in the 21st century, we must begin to conserve scarce resources, for instance, energy and other natural resources. We must attempt to conserve our land, clean water, and clean air. We must begin to conserve and use wisely our capital and human resources. I had hoped, perhaps naively, that this new Government might begin the task of introducing into the Canadian social and economic fabric some of the notions of a conserving society. How disappointed I was when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought down his economic statement.
It seemed to me that all the programs which the Liberals had introduced in a hesitant way, often as a result of pressure from people such as New Democrats, and I must say as well the odd Conservative Member, were some of the main programs which the Minister of Finance and the Conservative Party elected to cut back or abolish as a whole.
Let us go through the list. First, let me deal with environmental questions. Coming from Saskatchewan, I have been concerned with the increasing use of herbicides and pesticides. It has been the practice in the last number of years to use chemical products to kill weeds and undesirable pests. Over the years we find that insects and plants develop resistance to these chemical products, and so more powerful chemical products are needed to do the job. We have also found that some of the tests that determine the safety of these products on the environment and on consumers have not been all that honest.
A number of years ago I rose in my place in the House and brought to the attention of the former Minister of the Environment, the former Minister of Health, and the former Minister of Agriculture the faulty testing of International Bio-Test Laboratories in the United States. It had done most of the testing on almost all of the herbicides and pesticides that are on the market in Canada today. It was discovered that that lab had deliberately falsified the tests. The matter was first brought up in a Senate subcommittee by Senator Kennedy in the United States. I raised questions in the House and in committee on numerous occasions. In the beginning, the then Minister of Health pooh-poohed me. She said that I was unduly raising the concerns of Canadians and that our system of testing the safety of these products was quite adequate. Many officials of International Bio-Test Laboratories are in jail in the United States. The governments both in the United States and in Canada have had to withdraw certain products from the market because they were found unsafe. Tests had to be redone costing millions of dollars, for which farmers and consumers must eventually pay.
It has been recognized that the massive use of chemicals will have a detrimental effect on users, consumers, and the environment. Studies after studies have been done by the Department of the Environment showing mutations among the lower level of biological life at the lake bottoms in Saskatchewan and in the Great Lakes as a result of the chemical residue that washes into these fresh bodies of water.
Programs that monitor changes in the lower form of life give warning signals to the rest of society. They tell us that abnormal changes in the life pattern are occurring and these will eventually move up into life's chain, affecting the health and welfare of all Canadians. This monitoring is important if we are to conserve the fresh water we have for the generations to come. The speed of technological change is such that it is not just the health and safety of generations to come with which we must concern ourselves but the health and safety of our own generation.
I was very sad to notice that one of the programs to be cut by this Government was the program to study toxicology and the program to study the effects of dioxins and other such substances in the Great Lakes.
A number of years ago I had the privilege together with my colleagues of touring the dump sites at Niagara on both the Canadian and the American sides. I saw the Love Canal. I am speaking not only of the Love Canal; there are other dump sites in which Hooker Chemical has dumped thousands of pounds of highly toxic materials. When the war in Vietnam came to an end, Hooker Chemical realized it had un-needed chemicals, such as Agent Orange. One will recall that DDT was banned. Hooker Chemicals decided to bury their un-needed chemicals in dump sites. We know there has been a certain amount of leeching from these dump sites through the Niagara River into the Great Lakes. We know there are toxic chemi-
December 3, 1984

cals in the dump sites. If some irresponsible person or some act of nature such as a storm, an earthquake, or whatever else were to wash enough of these highly toxic substances into the Great Lakes system, it would destroy the system as a source of fresh water for humans. The whole of the Great Lakes could become so filled with toxic substances that human beings would no longer be able to draw from it water to drink. It is so sad for me to hear that the program to monitor the amount of dioxin material in the Great Lakes is scrapped. I call that false economy. In fact, to say false economy is mild. It is such stupidity that it amazes me. For the sake of a few million dollars, the Government is willing to risk the water supply for all of southern Ontario. That is stupidity to the nth degree.
As a country we have one of the richest forms of natural wildlife. Today I received a letter from The Saskatchewan Natural History Society. I should like to read a paragraph of it for the record. It reads:
In particular our members are most outraged by cuts which will: close the Prairie Wildlife Interpretation Centre near Swift Current; halt the planned reintroduction of the Swift Fox, an endangered species; and cancel the 1985 opening of Grasslands National Park. Our members also wish to protest: reduction of wildlife research programs; elimination of the wildlife habitat acquisition fund and the termination of the 200 seasonal naturalist positions in National Parks.
This Government, previous governments and governments to come have a responsibility to preserve our wildlife so that it is not dissipated within the life span of our generation. It is terrible for us in this generation to assume that we can despoil wildlife for generations to come. Surely we have a responsibility and a duty to maintain our natural wildlife. The actions of the Government for the sake of saving a few million dollars have determined that the Swift Fox as an endangered species can go by the way and that the Grasslands National Park can go by the way, that there is no need to preserve them. What false economy!
Turning to the list of further cut-backs, I should like to deal with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. As we move into a time when energy will cost more because it is an unrenewable resource, even though market conditions will see the price fluctuate, we know that in the end the price and cost of energy will rise.
The solution for reasonable men and women is to begin to preserve, conserve and develop alternatives. With a downturn in the cost of energy such as the one we are experiencing now because of international situations and a downturn in the economy, we have been provided with a bit of breathing room. Now is the time to have on stream some of the alternatives- solar, wind and different forms of hydro. It is essential for us to make these alternatives into economically viable alternatives while there is time. Let us not awaken one morning to find another oil crisis where the cost of energy will go through the roof and threaten the economic and social well-being of the country. Let us not discover that we have not done our work on developing alternatives. Lo and behold, it is another area which the Government has deemed to be unuseful and deserves
Supply
to be cut. The NRC program developing wind, solar and alternative forms of energy is cut. The home insulation program is cut and will eventually die. That particular program saved the skin of the previous government and of Canadian taxpayers by the amount of energy it saved. Positive-thinking Canadians participated in that program. Governments at the time called upon Canadians to work together to help preserve and conserve energy, and Canadians responded. Surely that is the road the Government must follow if it really believes in working with people and being dedicated to conserving and preserving.
No, that is not the route the Government wants to see Canadians develop. Instead, we will become more dependent upon the oil industry and upon those people who hold the economic and social well-being of our country in their fists. Rather than encouraging and providing leadership for Canadians to develop alternatives and independence, we will be forced into a greater dependency upon the oil industry.
Turning to the area of housing, again I refer to the work of the National Research Council in developing more energy-efficient housing. That program will be scrapped. RRAP attempts to conserve and preserve older housing stock in the city core. That program has been cut. Our city cores can rot. As long as land developers and speculators on the outskirts of cities are doing their thing, everything must be hunky-dory as far as the Tories are concerned. So much for the core of our cities.
Let me deal with the cuts in cultural agencies. Wise men and women who have the responsibility of government must realize that if we are to preserve ourselves as an independent country, having our own sense of identity and culture and living so close to the American border and its culture, it is the responsibility of governments to work with the private sector to help maintain and conserve a separate cultural identity. This is why cultural activities are so essential for the well-being of our nation as a separate entity. However, we see further cut-backs in essential cultural services to the country.
The Tories say, "preserve it" and "conserve it"; in fact, that was their slogan in Ontario. In fact, they ran Ontario Hydro ads reading "preserve it, conserve it". The previous speaker from Kootenay West made reference to George Orwell. I would like to do likewise. Surely Newspeak is occurring here, the utterance of slogans which in the end are just empty slogans. The government Party is not committed to preserving and conserving. It is committed to exploitation. It is committed to exploiting the environment here and now and damn the future, damn the environment, damn the quality of life and the quality of our fresh water. It is not a conserving Party. It is one that exploits, one that would seek to exploit our valuable human, technological and environmental resources just for its sake right now. It is not concerned with the future. It is not composed of men and women who have the well-being of generations to come at heart. Its bottom line is whether its members will be re-elected in four years. Its time span is a very narrow one. As we move into the 21st century, I am afraid it is a mind-set which will lead to disasters such as the urea formaldehyde disaster, thalidomide babies, environmental

mistakes, miscalculations and misplanning. Future generations will have to pay many more dollars to correct the mistakes that these people are making in the name of false economy. As such, I wholeheartedly support this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. He has advocated expenditure on a number of items which have been postponed. Would he prefer a larger deficit this year than previously announced by the Liberals? Would he like to spend forever?

Mr. Speaker, I have given two speeches in this House dealing with the deficit. I am well on record as saying that the deficit has to be reduced. I have been suggesting that there are false economies. I suggest that these cuts in the environment, science and preventive health care are false economies that will in the end cost us more.
The point in both my speeches is that this Government is concerned about the expenditure side of the balance sheet. The Economic Council reported last week that the Canadian Government has not overspent. As the Economic Council pointed out, we have not been collecting the revenues that should have been collected.
I pointed out the scam in the research and development tax credit. Introduced by our Liberal friends, it was supposed to involve only $100 million in lost revenue. When the Liberals left, it had run up to $1.5 billion. Apparently there is a grandfather clause. We will lose another $400 million to $500 million under the Tories because of this grandfather clause. Instead of putting on a moratorium, we will lose another half billion dollars under this grandfather clause. That half billion dollar loss would do more than just restore these cut-backs in the environment, preventive health care and home insulation.
That is why my answer to the Hon. Member is that these cuts are false economies. The public Treasury could have saved money in ways they have chosen to ignore. Rather, they cut areas that are essential to the health and well-being of Canada.

No, Mr. Speaker, I have not given a counterbudget. As soon as the Government introduces its full budget, there will be opportunities to introduce a counterbudget. I have suggested one item to the Hon. Member: Put the freeze on the grandfather clause that deals with R and D. That would save the public Treasury some $500 million. With that saving, the Government could restore some of the cut-backs in preventive health care, home insulation, alternate energy and the environment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: Does the Hon. Member not believe that he would gain credibility if he suggested, rather than just criticising, a constructive alternate package of cuts and tax increases?

Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. That is why we will be asking the Government for much more information. We want to know about the $4.5 billion in uncollected taxes. We want to know whether the $1.6 billion that the corporate sector has not paid in taxes, even though it accepts the fact that it owes these taxes, has been collected. We want to know why the $400 million which companies have deducted from their employees to be remitted to the Government has not been remitted. Why is the Government writing off $100 million of that amount?
We want to know some of the deferred taxes. We want to know the type of information introduced by the Minister of Finance in the Clark Government with regard to tax loopholes and how much lost revenue has occurred. We would like to know how many jobs were created and how much useful social activity occurred because of these tax breaks. When we have that information, we will be able to supply the Hon. Member with a blueprint of how to balance our budget and still do the important things a Government needs to do, such as conserving the health and the environment of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to be sure I heard the Hon. Member correctly. A moment ago he said he wanted to balance the budget. Is it now the position of the New Demo-cratid Party that it wants to have a balanced budget?

Mr. Speaker, it would be very foolish for us to attempt to balance the budget in one year. It would create social havoc. Let me point out, as I have done in other speeches-and the Hon. Member may not be aware of this- that when the NDP and its predecessor the CCF were the government of the Province of Saskatchewan, we had a balanced budget. When the Conservatives were elected in the Province of Saskatchewan in 1982, we had a surplus of $170 million. After less than two years of Conservative government, the Province of Saskatchewan has a deficit higher that all the deficits in the history of Sasktachewan rolled into one, thanks to a Conservative government. How they were able to accomplish that is still a puzzle to us. They cut back on social and human services and sold mines, highway equipment and public assets. They have done the cut-backs and have still rolled up a $1 billion deficit. That takes some doing.
Why is it that Conservative governments, whether elected in England, the United States or Saskatchewan, end up with higher deficits than ever before? The highest deficit in the United States is now, under a Conservative government. The highest deficit in England is now, under a Conservative government. The highest deficit in Saskatchewan is now, under a Conservative government.
I will stand here in my place one, two and three years from now and accuse this Government of increasing our deficit. I predict that with its economic policies there will be a downturn in economic development in this country, in economic activity.

Public revenues will fall and the deficit will increase under its so-called stewardship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased that the Hon. Member stopped at the end of three years because in the fourth year we hope that he will be defeated. Under the NDP Government of Manitoba, the only NDP Government we have presently, that Province has the highest per capita deficit of any province. It started under Sterling Lyon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: This is much higher. The Hon. Member did not answer my question. How soon does he want to see the federal budget balanced?

Mr. Speaker, we all want to see our debts paid off as soon as possible. As I mentioned before, this cannot be done overnight. We have to accept some of the economic realities. We have to ensure that cuts are done with wisdom, care and in an open way. People should know the economic and social consequences of those cuts. That is how to begin to reduce the deficit. We must pinpoint where there are wasteful expenditures and where there are tax breaks and tax loopholes that are not productive. Once that information becomes public, it will become evident to all Members of Parliament and Canadians where the fat is to be trimmed, what loopholes are to be closed and what public revenues are to be saved. Until the Government comes across and starts supplying that information rather than trying to hide it in some secretive way, Canadians, including members of the Opposition, will never be able to give a straight answer to the Hon. Member because we do not have the information. The Government has the information and it does not want to share it with anybody.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Guilbault (Saint-Jacques);
That this House regrets that, after less than three months in office, the Government is in growing disarray as demonstrated by its harmful, inadequately considered and irresponsible cuts in government services of importance to the economic and social development of the regions and of individual Canadians as well as by Ministers' apparent inability to manage their departments and their relations with the provinces and with the public.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be taking part in the debate today and to second the motion moved by my colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault).
I would like to start by mentioning the presence in the Chair of the newly elected Member for Vercheres (Mr. Danis) who has been a patient and courageous defender of Progressive Conservative interests in the Province of Quebec for many years, and I am sure it gives him a great deal of satisfaction to be here in the House.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore wish to offer you my best wishes for a successful though perhaps not very long career.
This Government, which has just received a very strong mandate from the Canadian people, started by creating expectations among all levels of our society. It is a fact that Canada is going through a difficult economic period. Because of the world economic situation, unemployment rates in this country have been fairly high, and, like other industrialized countries, we have also experienced a slowdown in economic growth.
At the time it was easy for the Opposition to criticize the Government and have Canadians believe that a change in government would be beneficial. However, we accept the verdict of Canadian voters. The Progressive Conservative Party offered Canadians an alternative, which was accepted. Voters thought that by electing Progressive Conservative Members, prosperity would return to this country and they would find jobs very shortly. We do not blame them for this political judgement. We are too democratic to complain about the result of an election. We accept the people's verdict, but, as the Official Opposition, it is our duty to point out to Canadians that this Government, which promised so much, is very slow to deliver on its promises and to respond to the expectations of Canadians.

I was reading the newspaper "Le Droit" and I saw a headline: "All talk, no action". I am referring to an editorial by journalist Alain Dexter, which appeared in the weekend edition. He was referring to the Government of Canada in connection with acid rain and said: "All talk, no action".
Mr. Speaker, I think this is an appropriate slogan for the new Government of Canada and its Prime Minister: "All talk and no action", because the Progressive Conservative Party's 338 election promises are certainly far from being kept, and I have no hesitation in saying right now that they will never be kept in the four years to come. All we have to do is look at what has been done, starting with the Throne Speech, and then the economic message by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), to realize that this Government has already aligned itself with certain groups in our society, to the detriment of those Canadians who are in need and constitute the most disadvantaged groups in our society. If anyone asked me what kind of favorites this Government plays, I would say without hesitation that this Progressive Conservative Government, this Mulroney Government, plays favorites with big business and more particularly, with the oil companies.
If we read the economic message carefully, in page after page the Minister of Finance focussed almost exclusively on energy questions, not for the benefit of Canadian consumers but for the benefit of the multinationals which are being given additional grants and additional concessions. And who is going to pay? Canadian consumers, who will have to pay more for gas and oil in the months and years to come. This Government had raised a lot of hope and paid close attention to the people of Canada, this Government had stated that job creation would be its first priority, yet this same Government has just shown through budget cutbacks that it will create unemployment rather than jobs for Canadians.
This morning, I listened to the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise), his maiden speech in the House. And what did the Member for Chambly say? He told us that the Government has a three-prong action plan: first, lower the deficit, second, ask the private sector to create jobs and, third, invite foreign investors to spur our economy.
Closer examination of those three points reveals that the Canadian Government has given up altogether on its responsibilities. It expects others to create jobs and launch the economic recovery. Not only will the Government fail to create jobs but, as a result of its drastic cutbacks in several departments, it will create unemployment directly by making Canadian public servants lose their jobs and, indirectly, by depriving Canadian institutions of the grants they had become used to, which they were entitled to and which they were given before by the Liberal Government.
Quite obviously, Mr. Speaker, the Government has switched priorities, anxious as it is to lower the deficit. That is what
leading businessmen and major corporations have been saying for years to the Canadian Government, and that is what they told us when we were in office: Cut the deficit.
I have never seen an ordinary worker, an ordinary citizen, somebody we refer to as the man in the street urge the Government to cut the deficit. Never! But I have seen many business leaders, businessmen and major corporation executives tell the Government to cut the deficit. Well, now, the first priority of the Progressive Conservative Government, its first measure is not to give jobs to those who need them. No, its first priority is to reduce the deficit, to make ordinary Canadians suffer even more just to please the corporate sector. That is why I say that the favourable prejudice of the Mulroney Government benefits the corporate sector to the detriment of ordinary Canadians. We in the Official Opposition will work hard and tirelessly to force the Government to keep the election promises it made this past summer and in early September. We will make sure that people across the land come to understand and recognize this Government's true character, this new character that clearly will honour some commitments to the large multinational corporations but will not help all those whom they had promised to help during the election campaign.
We are now convinced that this will be detrimental to this country's poor, to the co-operative groups that are cut from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation's programs. It will be detrimental to the Canadian workers who welcomed the passing of the Canadian Labour Code Amendment Bill just before the Houses adjourned, and who now hear from the new Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) that time will be needed to draft the regulations and that the new amendments to the Canadian Labour Code will not become effective before a couple of years.
Mr. Speaker, this proves one thing. It proves that this Tory Government is not lending its ears to women and workers who were the main beneficiaries of the amendments to the Canadian Labour Code. This Government lends its ears to large corporations, to business people. Those bankers, those spokesmen for the Canadian Bankers' Association and the major Canadian manufacturers have told the Minister of Labour: "Sit on the regulations, wait before you put into force that Act which was passed by the previous Government. Take your time drafting the Regulations." And this Tory Government, with an ear of course for these businessmen and bankers, has shelved as far away as possible the drafting of the new regulations relating to the Canadian Labour Code.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this is not good enough. It is sheer irresponsibility for the new Government not to draft as a priority the regulations under the Canadian Labour Code amendments. This amounts to penalizing thousands of Canadian women who need those new regulations in order to have justice on the market place. This amounts to penalizing thousands of Canadian workers employed in businesses under the

jurisdiction of the Canadian Government and who need those regulations as soon as possible to be better protected on the market place. Knowing the large number of occupational accidents in Canada, knowing the number of hours lost due to such accidents, I cannot understand why this Government does not want to immediately implement the regulations needed to better protect Canadian men and women in the work place.
Finally, I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a Government is very quickly judged according to what it does or does not do in the early stages of its mandate. As far as we are concerned, we very soon realized that this Government does not care for the people living in the most remotest parts of this country. People living in the most underprivileged areas have been the first hit by the cuts announced by the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I need only look at the programs affected, like the dairy policy.
If there is one group of Canadians in need of Government assistance, it is our Canadian farmers, especially those who work hard under difficult conditions, rising very early in the morning to take care of their dairy farms. Yet, as a result of Government action there will be cutbacks in our dairy programs. I find this completely unacceptable.
Secondly, this government is going to cut funds appropriated to social housing. Is there any thing more unfortunate than the situation of our senior citizens or simple people, living on an inadequate income, who are unable to find decent housing in many regions of Canada? Yet, the first message given by the new Government to these people is that there will be cutbacks in its social housing programs, which means that the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not be able to build facilities for senior citizens or social housing units so essential in our Canadian economy to provide assistance to the poorest and most disadvantaged members of our society.
In addition, the Government is preparing to cancel our job mobility programs. Because it is difficult to find work nowadays, the previous Liberal Government had implemented a subsidy program whereby Canadians could move to other parts of the country where jobs are available. However, this program, under which assistance was provided to workers willing to move to other regions where jobs were available, has been cancelled by this Government. In my opinion, this goes directly against the interests of Canadian workers who are looking for jobs.
Finally, we have been told that job creation programs for young people and summer employment programs for students will be cancelled. This is another group in our society which needs Government assistance and which has been deceived and let down by this Progressive Conservative Government in the very first days of its administration.
I shall close by saying that it does not take long to judge a new Government, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian people certainly

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address this House for the first time.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I look forward to the opportunity over the next three to four years of addressing and contributing to the process that takes place in this House in a meaningful and positive manner.
During the recent election campaign, the Progressive Conservative Party promised Canadians an enlightened national program for economic renewal, a program built on a solid foundation of open consultation with the provinces, the private sector, management and labour, women's groups, natives and minorities. We promised to build a dynamic national consensus that would define new national goals for Canada and a fair and equitable manner in which they could be realized. In the three short months since Canadians overwhelmingly endorsed our manifesto, we outlined, on November 8, the first chapter of a coherent national plan to involve Canadians in determining their collective destiny. It was a courageous effort, open, detailed, sound, logical and, above all else, honest. It is a plan that will give Canadians an opportunity to participate in a consultative and co-operative process that will lead to a rekindling of a vast potential which was kept dormant by the years of virtually uninterrupted Liberal mismanagement and frivolous abuse of their elected position. What the Liberal government of the last decade and a half failed to do, we have done in three short months.
The program of expenditure reductions announced on November 8 were part of a conscious, well defined plan for economic renewal, Mr. Speaker. They were not arbitrary, heavy-handed and callous reductions in government expenditure as suggested by the Hon. Member in his motion. They involved numerous responsible discussions between Ministers who took great care to ensure that no single group of Canadians or no single region was disproportionately affected. We were ever mindful that all expenditure reductions were not without some degree of pain. At the same time we were steadfast in our belief that some bitter medicine was needed to revitalize a great Canada left moribund by Liberal mismanagement and imprudence.
We were not alone in the belief that expenditure reductions were needed and could be effectively introduced. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) himself admitted during the campaign that there were billions of dollars in the current $100 billion federal budget being wasted. He said, and I quote:
There is a lot of space to reduce and cut expenditures and duplications. Programs which are no longer in force, which are no longer pertinent, wastage in public administration. 1 believe this reduction in expenditures could save us billions of dollars.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, federal Government spending has climbed from around $12 billion in 1968 to over $100 billion in 1984. A significant portion of this increase occurred in the four years since 1980. Government spending was only $50
Supply
billion when the Liberals were re-elected in 1980. The profligacy that followed in those short four years was unparalleled in recent history and is a matter of public record and public discontent. The last 10 years since 1974-75 has been characterized by a staggering accumulation in our public debt as the result of annual deficits, and I would like to examine briefly some of the facts.
In 1974-75, the net public debt was $24 billion. By the end of 1984-85, it will have risen to almost $190 billion, an eight-fold increase in 10 short years. In 1974-75, $1 out of every $20 of tax revenue was used to pay the net interest on this debt. If gross interest payments were used, the numbers are one in three in 1984-85, compared to one in nine just 10 years ago. Canada's national debt is growing much faster than the Canadian economy. The net public debt will have increased from 16.6 per cent of the Gross National Product in 1974-75, to a whopping 45.2 per cent in the current year. If allowed to grow as projected, by 1990-91 the net public debt will have more than doubled to $400 billion, or 63 per cent of the projected Gross National Product.
These continuing deficits and growing debt critically undermine confidence. They put upward pressure on interest rates and reduce prospects for growth, not to mention the psychological albatross around the necks of future generations of Canadians. Simply put, if taken all at once, then total deficit would cost each Canadian taxpayer over $17,000, more than many Canadians make in a whole year, Mr. Speaker.
The persistence of deficits, while eroding the confidence of foreign and domestic investors, is also indicative of the previous government's inability to manage its financial affairs with any degree of prudence. This Government cannot and must not tolerate the continuation of such a pattern of excessive expenditures relative to revenue. In behaving responsibly and practically, we introduced a number of very conscious policy and program decisions on November 8. The decisions were aimed at restoring some degree of fiscal flexibility within the context of creating an environment within which balanced and sustained growth could be fostered.
The Hon. Member has referred to harmful and irresponsible cuts and makes wild allegations regarding the relationship of this Government to the provinces and the public. We are all aware that government has become too big under too many years of Liberal mismanagement. With its regulations, subsidies and interventions, it intrudes perversely into the lives of Canadians and the Canadian market-place. Heaven help the poor unsuspecting Canadian business person who endeavours to find his way through the maze of over 100 federal government programs which purport to serve his needs.
During the campaign, Mr. Speaker, this Party promised to introduce principles of productive government management to ensure that Canadian taxpayers received value for money. To make government more responsive to the needs and aspirations of Canadians, we launched the ministerial task force on program review led by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen). Its mandate is to streamline the delivery of programs, to eliminate duplication, and to get more value for every dollar

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to rise today to speak to this motion put forward by the Liberal Party. I believe that the motion demonstrates the absolute moral bankruptcy of that Party. I knew that before the election but now I am convinced of it today.
The Liberals have the audacity to criticize us about government spending and our relations with the provinces and the public. It is unimaginable how the Liberals can condemn us after 20 years of spending public money like drunken sailors and inflating the deficit to $30 billion. We are attempting to deal with the problems which the Liberals have left with us.
How did today's problems come about and what can we do to solve them? The economic and fiscal mismanagement which has resulted in our record deficit began in the early and mid 1970s when the Minister of Finance at that time, the present Hon. Leader of the Opposition, talked about the need for restraint. During the five budgets that he introduced, federal government spending doubled, a $600 million surplus was transformed into a $4 billion deficit, and the net debt grew by 50 per cent. Public debt charges doubled, and the Public Service grew by 74,000, excluding cuts to the Armed Forces.
The Auditor General of Canada stated that Parliament had lost or was losing effective control of the public purse. According to a study by the C.D. Howe Institute at that time, three of the five budgets of the then Minister of Finance actually widened the gap between rich and poor. This is the legacy that we have inherited.
Following that auspicious beginning, the Liberal government continued another ten years of spending money, increasing the deficit and building a spirit of confrontation in this country, the likes of which we have never seen before. This is the legacy that we are now attempting to deal with as the Government.
The economic renewal strategy plan that was announced in the Throne Speech refers to removing impediments to growth, seeking national consensus for economic direction, reinvigorating investment, and enhancing private sector risk-taking and innovation among entrepreneurs.
In immediately attempting to reduce the huge federal deficit, this administration has realized that the cost of servicing
the deficit limits the Government's ability to meet priority economic and social needs. The deficit hides the real cost of government and does not allow for society's response to the needs of its citizens. The deficit inhibits private sector growth and constrains the Government's ability to encourage growth.
I am convinced that the most constructive role that our Government can play is to concentrate its attention on creating a kind of environment in which the private sector can do what it does best-to create jobs and new prosperity. Increasing private sector confidence and investment in the Canadian economy will result in the security of employment and jobs.
I suggest it is fair to ask why the deficit needs to be addressed. NDP members, including the NDP spokesman on industrial regional development, who claims to be an economist by profession, seemed unable to analyse what has happened to our country in the last 15 years of continued deficits. The Government, just like any business or individual, faces the problem of financing a debt when it spends more than it takes in. When the Government runs a deficit, it has two sources of financing. The first is the printing of money. The second source is borrowing. Both sources have inherent problems that eventually result in a weaker economy and the loss of jobs.
Let me explain briefly how this happens for the benefit of some Members who seem unable to make that link. In the early years of deficits, the governments resorted to printing money. The basic result was an expanding money supply and an ever-increasing inflation, which essentially robs the workers and those on fixed incomes of their spending power. In fact, it is a hidden tax.
The second method of financing is deficit borrowing. There are two sources of borrowing-foreign and domestic. Since the government must pay the interest and possibly repay the principal on a foreign debt, the result is pressure on the Canadian dollar. That pressure must be balanced by the Bank of Canada through such measures as an inflated interest rate. Canadians have seen the result of inflated interest rates in the last few years. The majority of federal government borrowing is done domestically. That domestic borrowing has a drastic economic effect because essentially it removes the available capital in this country and crowds out private borrowing. It raises the cost of money, which is, in essence, the interest rate.
Money is just like any other commodity. When there is an increased demand for money by the government, interest rates are driven up and foreign borrowing is crowded out.
Furthermore, we are all familiar with the very negative effect of high interest rates. We have witnessed how high interest rates have resulted in a decline in consumer spending for those high ticket items such as cars and housing which produce many jobs in this country. High interest rates are also very detrimental to small businesses which require sources of capital at a cost that will not prevent a new business from realizing a profit.
The job of rebuilding the Government's finances and implementing policies that will support economic growth and job creation is just beginning. We asked Canadians for this oppor-

tunity and we are absolutely delighted that we received such a strong national mandate for change. Canadians from all regions and from all groups expressed through their votes the belief that our country could and indeed had to do better.
I represent a western riding and therefore must travel extensively. I have talked to people in airports as well as to my constituents and have heard nothing but positive support for the direction in which the Government is heading. While I have received some correspondence at my office expressing some concern about individual cuts in spending or about programs that have been affected, most individuals realize that despite their concern, the Government had to control its spending and get its house in order. While these people may have asked for a review of their individual case, they essentially agree with the objectives of the Government.
The fact is that we have support for our policies. I believe that that is borne out by opinion polls, much to the dismay of our friends on the opposite side of the House. They are aware that Canadians acknowledge our progress and that we have their confidence. Canadians voted for a change in policies and in the approach of Government to the making of policy. This motion today is trying to tell us to go back to the old ways, the old ways of a government that had been spending money like a drunken sailor, spending it on a political basis aimed at ridings held by Liberal Members. One of my colleagues mentioned that the way to attack problems by the former government was to set up commissions so its friends could be well looked after, travel the world at taxpayers' expense and live, I think the words were, "reasonably comfortably". And what about the probe into the Gimli airplane case-

This nation is seriously in debt, Mr. Speaker. Business confidence has ebbed. Foreign investors have been scared off and unemployment is painfully high. As soon as the election was called, everyone knew what was going to happen. People did not have to wait. People knew the Liberal govern-
Supply
ment was going to be turfed out. In the third quarter, we had a dramatic 8 per cent increase in our GNP. Just the fact that the election was called inspired confidence in a new government that everyone knew was going to be elected.
The Government can neither wish nor legislate economic growth and meaningful job opportunities into being. The way must be made clear for the private sector to become confident, to flourish, to invest, and thus to create jobs. The Government must move step by step to remove a wide range of obstacles to growth and new jobs. The private sector must be provided with a stable and comprehensive policy environment. The first order of business is to take action on the deficit. The mounting federal debt has become the single most powerful obstacle to growth and private sector job creation. It has been said that the greatest financial invention was compound interest. From an investment point of view, this may be true, but there is another side to compound interest, that seen by the debtor. The federal Government, unfortunately, has fallen into massive indebtedness that now feeds on itself. New interest charges generate new borrowings, which lead to more and more interest charges, an accelerating treadmill of debt.
Even with relatively favourable assumptions about interest rates and continuing economic growth, the deficit in future years was projected to remain in the range of $34 to $38 billion. On the one hand it was clear that we would not just grow our way out of the deficit problem. We could not spend our way out. In fact, we would be getting into an even greater debt problem unless we took action. The public debt, if left unchecked, would reach a staggering total of $410 billion by the end of this decade, the equivalent of $54,000 for every Canadian family. Each year we are borrowing more and more money just to pay the interest on past debts. In so doing, we are imposing a crippling tax burden on future generations.
When, as is currently the case, more than $1 out of every $3 of tax revenue is used to pay the interest on the national debt, then it is clear we are not only compounding past debts, we are compromising the future. The accumulating debt threatens the creation of permanent jobs for unemployed Canadians today and for our children in the years to come, and it does so in a number of different ways. It puts upward pressure on interest rates by raising the expectations of future inflation and by competing for private savings. It limits the Government's ability to meet priority economic and social needs. It symbolizes a state of economic mismanagement that undermines confidence and threatens the job-creating private investment that Canada needs.
That is why, despite the limited time available, the Government had to make a number of tough decisions which were announced on November 8 as part of the economic statement, decisions to reduce expenditures and to increase revenue recovery as a first step in controlling the deficit. As a result of these measures, the projected deficit for 1985-86 has been brought down to $34.9 billion from the projected $37.1 billion. Those figures tell us that much more needs to be done. Clearly, this will not be an easy or a painless task. Some pain, as mentioned

by the motion, has already been felt, but we will have to feel a lot more in trying to correct this mess.
What is this?

As we did with our initial spending reductions, we will continue to do our best to ensure that our decisions are consistent with all our economic renewal objectives, including the principles of greater self-reliance for the private sector and equitable treatment for all regions of the country, not just Conservative or Liberal regions. We will even help NDP regions a little. We will treat NDP regions fairly as well.
Of course, we could have responded to the debt problem differently. One option would have been to try to treat the situation with stimulative financing. Yet nothing short of a massive injection of stimulus would have had any initial effect on growth or employment. With the deficit for this year already $5 billion higher than was projected in last February's Budget, deliberate and massive stimulation would have left us in a very precarious position. The country would have sunk more deeply into the quagmire of national debt, and long-run prospects for growth and employment would have been seriously harmed. The cost in lost investor and consumer confidence would have lost us jobs in future years.
The other option we had was to chop the deficit dramatically and ruthlessly right at the start. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that many of my constituents have told me that that is what we should have done. But this Draconian appproach would have undermined confidence and threatened social cohesion. The costs of adjusting to such a sudden wrench in the economy would have been high, and our collective ability to deal with our structural problems would have been undermined.
We must do all we can to encourage a more dynamic and self-reliant private sector. We must deal not only with the deficit, but also with the tangled web of regulations, subsidies and other forms of government intervention that have been built up over the years.
Too many industries in this country are overprotected. Too many programs designed to assist investment have distorted investment decisions and encouraged the establishment of companies viable only with continued taxpayer support. Too many negative signals have been sent to foreign investors, particularly in the energy sector, and too many government programs carry on long after they have stopped being needed.
In short, the inherent dynamism of the Canadian economy has been eroded by frequently inappropriate and erratic economic policies.
Besides changing government policies, we need to change the way we go about the public's business. We need to take the confrontational tension out of the air which was the hallmark of past governments. We need to sit down and talk to one another.
We have challenged all Canadians to take a hard look at fundamental problems and to break free of the conventional wisdom of the past. The challenge is great for all of us, but particularly so for the private sector. The private sector must
be the driving force behind growth and job creation. I think we in this Government are on our way to giving Canadians the kind of confidence they can and should have in their government.

Mr. Speaker, I am amazed to hear repeated Conservative speakers who have addressed the motion before us today saying that they are looking for options. Perhaps they should consider the option which they promised the Canadian electorate several months ago. Also we have heard them talk repeatedly about their top priority being deficit cutting.
In my riding the candidate for that Party never touched the question about deficit cutting. He stressed job creation. I asked an Hon. Member who spoke previously what kind of initiatives would be brought forth in order to create jobs and how they would maintain the fundamental promise which they made from coast to coast during the election campaign.
If I look at my own city in North York, I see quite the opposite. I see the Government cutting a $58 million tax centre which would have created 3,000 jobs-2,000 full-time and
1,000	part-time. It would have created hundreds of jobs in the construction and trade industries. It would have provided a service to the citizens of North York. Where was the job initiative in that cut? Where were the promises to Canadians before September 4 about the multitude of cuts we have witnessed? What happened to the Government on the way to the House of Commons after September 5?
I do not want to hear from the Hon. Member anything about deficit cuts because we did not hear anything about them during the campaign. We heard about job-creation programs which would come overnight from the Government. I would like to hear what the Hon. Member has to say in terms of actual numbers of jobs being created. That is what Canadians want to hear.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to respond to both those points. First he talked about deficit reduction during the election campaign. I assure him that I used every opportunity to talk about deficit reduction. I said that deficit reduction was the only way to get true job creation. I was not referring to job creation in terms of make-work projects using the money of the government and taxpayers. The only way to obtain permanent, long-lasting and meaningful jobs is through job creation by the private sector.
For example, in the job-creation programs which we have funds have been allocated in an attempt to provide people with meaningful jobs and to use that money in the best possible way. That is in contrast to the former government. I am talking about the Canada Works program. For the last several years, my riding has received the minimum allocation under the Canada Works program of $100,000 per year. The reason we continued to receive it was that the former government continued to manipulate the formulas and to use data which were three to five years old to arrive at its formulas. In actual fact, ridings which could rightfully call upon those funds were

refused their fair share simply because Conservative Members were representing them.
Under the Canada Works program, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), in allocating funds, used current data so that it would be done on a fair basis. In my riding, the amount of funds received rose from $100,000 to $770,000 this year. A large number of projects is being evaluated by the advisory board. We hope to have some good jobs.
Despite the fact that we have to do that temporarily because of the current situation, those programs are not the answer. I hope that in two, three or perhaps four years from now those programs will not be around any longer. They are simply a band-aid solution. They are not a long-term solution. We have to create true jobs in the private sector. The only way to do that is by giving the private sector room within which to work, and the only way to do so is by reducing the federal Government deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure how a short, succinct question could do justice to the many myths which were put before the House by the last speaker.
Does the Hon. Member not think that it is important, in talking about the deficit in Canada, to recognize that the personal savings rate in this country is two and a half times that in the United States? Does he not think that it is also important to recognize that every conceivable authority concedes that no crowding out effect is taking place in an economy where investment has declined over the last two years and where there is idle capacity and excess unemployment? Does he not realize that there is no possible way that businesses could be faced with too much competition for funds? In short, is he not applying an argument about the deficit which might make sense in the United States but is entirely different here given the conditions in this country?

Mr. Speaker, certainly I realize that the personal savings rate in this country is very high. I will take the Hon. Member's word that it is two and a half times that in the United States. However, the reason it is high is the lack of consumer and investor confidence. People are paying down their debt. They are reluctant to spend it on consumer goods or on business investment because they are afraid of the federal Government deficit getting out of control and of not receiving a return on their money. In fact, they are afraid that there will be hyperinflation. Eventually the Government will have to pay its bill. If it cannot do it by borrowing, it will do it by printing money. Then we would see the kind of inflation which exists in Israel, and the money people have spent will come back to them in worthless dollars. That is the reason for the lack of confidence. We in the Government are trying to instil some confidence in the Canadian consumer and investor.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because other Members want to speak to this motion. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) on his excellent motion-"irresponsible cuts, Ministers' apparent inability to manage their Departments and their relations with the provinces and with the public." Of all that the Conservative Government promised, and still promises, it is consultation with the provinces, openness and the stop of those decisions made from on high in Ottawa.
One Member mentioned in this debate cuts in the social housing program. I want to elaborate on that issue as it relates to the lack of consultation with the provincial governments. They were not consulted. If there is one thing a government must do when it cuts back on social housing projects, it is to consult with the provincial governments and the agencies concerned.
The reason is quite simple. It is the provincial government agencies which have to guarantee the occupancy in most of the social program public housing in this country. The provincial governments decide when a housing project will be built and where. I know that CMHC has certain maneuvrability in its programs, but it is the provincial governments that have to act in concert with the federal government.
