In the last five years, each provincial government has announced a five-year program. It is common for a provincial government to have a five-year program from senior citizen homes, nursing homes and the like. This announced cut-back of $9.5 million in the social housing area will have an incredible effect on these plans. This $9.5 million may not sound like much money, but this is a cash cut from 1985 to 1986.
The social housing department of CMHC has ongoing responsibilities on 30 and 35 year mortgages. They cannot be stopped. We are looking at a financial cut for the year 1985-86. A senior citizens' home with a $4 million mortgage could pay an additional $100,000 to bring the rate of interest down 2 per cent. That kind of a cut right across this country will involve a substantial reduction in social housing programs right across this country. There was no consultation. I understand that the federal Minister responsible for housing will meet with his provincial counterparts later this week, after the decision was made and after it was handed down from on high by this Government. There was no consultation with provincial governments.
The other area that hits at the heart of the issue was the announced 25 per cent cut in RRAP. That really smacks of discrimination. It discriminates against the poorer regions of this country. This is another example of lack of consultation with the provinces. It is the provincial housing authorities which deliver the RRAP program in high unemployment areas. Apart from the national poverty organization in various high unemployment areas, the provincial housing authorities deliver this program.
I continually criticized the previous government for restricting this program. It started off as a great program. You could qualify depending on the condition of your house. It started to be restricted because the demand was so high and the money was just not there. It reached the point where a family of four could not put on the extra bedroom.
It began with a forgiveness of $3,750 for those whose income was below $11,000. It increased later to $5,000 for those whose income was below $13,500. The provincial housing authorities are now being told that this program is being cut back 25 per cent across the board. The provincial housing authorities, the delivery agents, do not know what to do. One housing authority I checked with said it will meet next week to decide on a public statement. It will not criticize the federal Government in that statement. It cannot do that.
Incredible cuts are being made in transportation with no consultation with the provincial governments affected. Some of these cuts are absolutely outrageous. The motion says they are irresponsible cuts. That is an understatement.
The tourism departments in each province have been working with the federal Government to try to devise a long-term plan to encourage tourism. The Provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island have always wanted a cheap ferry system. They demanded that. Each time CN Marine increased its rates, each provincial government filed an objection with the Canadian Transport Commission.
This Government has laid down in law that CN Marine must cut $20 million from its administration and operations. It is to cut a further $17 million in its gulf ferry runs and coastal boat service without consulting with the provincial governments. No sweat for CN Marine. It announced a 15 per cent rate increase and blamed it on the federal Government. The decision was handed down from on high with no consultation with the affected provincial governments.
One person and a car travelling from North Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Argentia, Newfoundland, must pay $98 or $99-I say it is $100-on the basis of a 15 per cent fare increase. Add to that a reduction in coastal boat service, which was never adequate, not on my coast of Newfoundland or on other coasts. That is the word from on high from this great Government that is going to consult and ensure that everything is open. That is what it has done with regard to transportation.
The Fisheries Loan Board is meeting this week in most of the provinces affected to determine what can be done as a result of the announcement made by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to cut out the national insurance scheme. These fisheries loan boards will have to seize some of the boats next year, have their own insurance scheme or have a subsidy or package arrangement delivered through the private insurance companies. Subsidizing private insurance companies is not in the statement of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He did not consult before the decision was made. He will now be consulting after the decision.
Other policies were announced which will substantially affect provincial budgets. There was no consultation. No one in this House can stand and say that provincial welfare budgets will not be affected by the $200 million cut-back in unemployment insurance. The reason is that it will be more than $200 million. The system which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) says she is going to put into effect will cut more than $200 million out of the unemployment insurance paid to Canadians. The reasons are quite simple. The restrictions on people drawing unemployment insurance in the country are too great as it is. If an unemployed person does not sit next to his or her telephone every day of the week for eight hours a day, he or she runs the risk of being cut off of unemployment insurance. I notice that the local unemployment offices in high-unemployment areas of the country have taken to heart what the Government has said and are making these phone calls as of two weeks ago. They are phoning fishermen on the northeast coast of Newfoundland asking where they were yesterday at 3 p.m. A fisherman might say: "I was down at the store," and the fellow says: "What store is that?" The fisherman then gives the name of some store in St. John's. The point is that this will affect the provincial governments.
The other part of this motion indicates that the Ministers do not really know what they are doing. On the subject of UIC, how does one cut back on the mobility program for people who

are looking for work in other parts of Canada? That mobility program is too tight right now. The people who need help from it cannot get it. Mr. Speaker, sitting as I do next to an economist from my own city, I hestitate to get into a discussion about deficits. However, having listened to the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin), who has unfortunately departed from the Chamber, I feel no hesitancy in stepping into waters in which I could not otherwise swim.
I may not know much about economics, but I do attempt to have some familiarity with history. I know that emphasis on deficits, notions of restraint and the cutting of social programs has had numerous precedents, not the least of which were the actions taken in the course of the Great Depression which made matters worse. I would suggest that could happen now. Even those people who are least informed about economic principles would understand that the great economic surge in the United States has resulted not from the actual implementation of what has been sloganed, but from the rather significant expenditures in the military area. That area has the function of creating make-work programs. Indeed, what we have is a model whereby one does not attempt to deal with the
December 3, 1984

deficit in the manner suggested by the Hon. Member who spoke previously, but on the basis that certain things can be accomplished by expenditures.
The issue is not one of idle economic speculation of Hon. Members on either side. What I have frequently noted in listening the Hon. Members opposite is that they seldom deal with the issue. They seem more determined to deal with their allegedly perfidious predecessors than with what they are responsible for. It is no wonder they have not chosen to deal with the motion before us.
The motion states that "the Government is in growing disarray". Can anyone seriously challenge the loss of government papers in hotel rooms, interviews in the form of dictation tapes, and contrary views about what regulations should apply to contracts with the press? I would suggest that that indicates there is some measure of disarray.
The motion goes on to suggest that the "growing disarray is demonstrated by its harmful, inadequately considered and irresponsible cuts in government services". Could anyone seriously suggest that the cuts in unemployment insurance will not prove harmful? Can there be any doubt about the harm that has been recognized in the cuts in environmental, scientific and cultural expenditures?
The motion states that the cuts were "inadequately considered". Let us for a moment reflect upon the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) and her reconsideration of ill-considered cuts, such as the herring gull project. A further example could be the hesitancy now evident with respect to CBC cuts. It is now recognized that they were a little too precipitous.
The motion goes on to suggest that there has been, on the part of the Ministers an "inability to manage their departments and their relations with the provinces and with the public". If Members opposite had been rational in their consideration of the content of this motion, they would have inevitably reached the conclusion that the resolution states the facts as they are.
1 really do regret that this kind of motion has appeared before us so early in the session. I was somewhat seduced by the proffering of the 300 promises made by the Leader of the Government during the election campaign. I suppose it reflected the fact that the Leader of the present Government was smiling as he made those promises. 1 should have recalled that his advisers had suggested he not laugh at his own jokes. Having observed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in these chambers, I would suggest that that advice is probably very useful-now knowing what the Government intends to do- because it may be thought by the poor that the Prime Minister is laughing at them.
We have a Government which promised there would be no confrontation. I suppose that has proven to be partly correct in the sense that the only confrontations of which this House is aware are confrontations over the previously mentioned policies with respect to contact of his Government with the press.
Supply
We have a Government which promised consultation. I believe every previous speaker referred to the lack of appropriate consultation with the provinces on a number of issues. But it seems to me there are other areas where there is a dangerous failure to consult. I have in mind the numerous actions taken with respect to science and technology. Clearly on the basis of any number of reports in the press, these decisions were taken without any consultation whatever. I cannot possibly believe that there could be no reaction from the government side unless those Hon. Members on the government side who are scientists have been muzzled. I cannot believe that scientists would have allowed such cuts as the herring gull project cut and the toxicology centre cuts, and so on.
We have a Government which has chosen only one of the two goals usually chosen for itself by society. On the one hand, there is the pursuit of social justice. On the other hand, there is the pursuit of prosperity and economic growth. Usually the people look to government to pursue the goal of social justice while it is the role of business to pursue the goal of economic growth and prosperity. It is obvious that this Government has chosen not to perform the proper function of government but to place its emphasis on the goals of business, thus separating social justice from the issue of prosperity and growth. This is marked by a whole litany of buzz words, one of which is "restraint", which really means, "let the poor eat confidence". We hear phrases like, "Cut the deficit. Cut unemployment insurance benefits. Cut government spending. Cut social programs". The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that every time there has been an attempt to cure the ills of society by pursuing prosperity at the expense of social justice, we have suffered. Every depression, every recession could be attributed in a very large measure to the fact that someone has chosen the route of abandoning social justice in the pursuit of prosperity at any price.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) said we must have short-term pain. As I look around me, I suspect there is not a soul in this room who is going to experience any pain whatsoever as the Government pursues this course. That Party talks a good game but it should experience the cuts in unemployment insurance benefits itself and try to cope, as does the lady who wrote to me recently saying she presently lives on $300 a month while paying $350 for housing and food.
This Government says that confidence is going to cure everything; let the poor eat confidence. But this Government is not even consistent. If it is going to pursue the kind of economic goal about which it talks, then one would have to consider the pillars of private sector growth. These pillars are research and development, innovation, technology diffusion, labour markets, human resources and adaptation to technological change. If one contemplates those so-called pillars, Mr. Speaker, then I believe one is driven to examine the economic statement, and the Government's agenda, and perhaps look for the steps which need to be taken in order to address the needs dictated by those pillars. One might contemplate the possibility of there being some reference to the necessity of having a broadly educated work force. One might look for suggestions

Supply
on how to increase the opportunities for young people, not in narrow, specified areas of training but with the kind of broad education and versatility which will be necessary for our economic future. One might have thought that Government would try to find some way to ensure that the offspring of the poor and of minorities would be encouraged to avail themselves of the kind of education which the great economic future which is promised will require. Yet nowhere in all of the verbosity which accompanied this great agenda does the Government deal with the issue of post-secondary education. There is some reference to transfer payments and this is elaborated upon, not in the documents themselves but in subsequent statements, to the effect that those transfer payments will have to be subject to restraint.
We have heard the glad tidings about youth. Youth are going to have an articulate spokesman. But in the economic statement we find that Summer Canada is to be cut by $85 million, and even that statement is misleading. That is the base funding. The fact is that the Government's so-called perfidious predecessor spent twice that amount on Summer Canada in 1983 and 1984.
We cannot have prosperity at the expense of the poor, the youth, single women, or minorities. We heard the Minister's reaction to the Abella report last week. There were vague phrases addressed to some 117 recommendations. But the Government could not see the forest for the trees, Mr. Speaker. If it looked at the clear recommendations of that report, it would realize that if we are to achieve justice for women, native people, the visible minorities and the disabled, there are certain specific actions which must be taken. Those actions certainly do have economic repercussions. But the Government casts aside any of those issues which have anything whatever to do with social justice in order to ensure that those who most strongly support the Government will benefit from whatever actions it may pursue in the interests of prosperity and that prosperity otherwise will dribble down to the rest of us.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-REQUEST THAT 1985 ENTRY LEVEL BE INCREASED
IMMIGRATION-REQUEST THAT 1985 ENTRY LEVEL BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is not in the House to hear what I have to say concerning the immigration target level of 85,000 to
90,000	set for 1985. I had expressed my feelings about its inadequacy, and I spoke not only for myself but on behalf of my Party which has announced itself in favour of a target for 1985 of at least 100,000.
The reason I am sorry the Minister is not here is that I wanted to explain to her how the target of 85,000 to 90,000 damages the reunification of families process. She did not seem to understand that, from the answers she gave to the questions I asked. She seemed to feel that all that was needed for families was to establish the relationship and they could immigrate.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, that is true as far as it goes but it is only true for immediate children, parents and grandparents of an individual Canadian applicant seeking to bring those family members to Canada. I was astonished the Minister did not know that the relatives who are wanted in Canada are not in that category. That is so in the great majority of cases I have in my office, and I am sure the same is true for all Members of Parliament. It is the brothers and sisters, sons and daughters who may be married or over the age of majority, nephews, nieces and others, who in every sense of the word, other than in the Minister's understanding, have to be considered to be family, and they ought to be able to be reunited in Canada, particularly at a time of economic growth.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the Government has admitted that it does not really know what to do. Why do 1 say that? The Minister herself said she felt more study was justified in deciding whether higher levels should be set for Canada's immigration target for 1985. If that is the way she feels about it, I urge the Government to keep the rate as it was, at least while these studies are being done. Do not lower it any further. It would be preferable to increase it recognizing that there is economic growth and that immigrants make a tremendous economic contribution in times of economic growth.
They do this in two ways, Mr. Speaker. First, they are consumers from the moment they arrive. It is winter in Canada now and they will need winter clothes. They need a place to live. They need to be fed. All of this puts extra demand in the Canadian economy. They have their families assisting them to become consumers when they first arrive.
Of course, much more important than their role as extra demand in the marketplace is the role they play and always have played in the labour market. They are the most willing workers in the country. They are anxious to establish themselves and obtain Canadian experience. I have always noted, in my years in business and in practice in Toronto, that immigrants are at least as willing as the rest of us to take any job to get started.
December 3, 1984

I regret very much that at a time when the Government itself is putting forward evidence of those who cannot get employees to do the jobs that need to be done in Canada, the Minister would take a hard-nose attitude towards immigrants.
Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister makes a determination of what the proper level is, that affects the way the Department operates around the world. If they are told that their target is lower, then the resources allocated are lower and the pace of work is less. In each of our immigration offices across the country there will be a less open attitude, rather than the more open attitude which there should be in a time of economic growth. That is very regrettable.
I note that according to the statutes, the Minister can come back as often as she wants to change that target. I would like her to reconsider that, as the Government has reconsidered so many of its mistakes in its first three weeks in Government. Let it reconsider this mistake also, and come back with an immigration level that is realistic, compassionate and humane in view of the immigration situation.
It was suggested that when I spoke today I should be very certain to speak to Canadians who themselves are not affected by immigration. Let us say there are some who do not have relatives they want to assist to come to Canada as immigrants. They should bear in mind that there must be someone around to pay their old age pensions when they reach 65 years of age. If one looks at the demographic studies, it will not be people who are born to the people already here who will pay. If we are going to have the kind of base population that we need to validate the commitments we are making to senior citizens and others in our society, we need more people in this country. The Liberal Party has always stood for those principles.
I am very disappointed that the Government has taken a kind of lead from the tough times of the last few years and put on the clamps. Let the minister and her hench persons reconsider that policy.

subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) DISCUSSIONS WITH JAPANESE CANADIAN COMMUNITY
VISIBLE MINORITIES-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) DISCUSSIONS WITH JAPANESE CANADIAN COMMUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the debate on this adjournment motion I would like to focus some attention on two questions I asked during Question Period on November 23. I appreciate that the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) has taken the time to come here this evening.

December 3, 1984
Adjournment Debate
As I mentioned earlier in the debate today, I was somewhat worried about the priority the Minister had given to the whole question of multiculturalism. I said in my earlier remarks that the Throne Speech in terms of multiculturalism was quite bankrupt. I feel strongly about that.
During the campaign of several months ago our various ethnocultural communities were promised a multicultural expressway to equal opportunity and greater facilitation in this whole process called Canada. Within that multicultural sphere I would like to concentrate this evening on those questions I asked concerning the Japanese-Canadian situation.
My questions were two-pronged. The first relates to the whole matter of an apology. The second is the issue of compensation. The Government has made this a priority. We were told during the campaign, and certainly following the campaign, that priority was to be given to the matter of apologizing to the Japanese Canadian community for the policy undertaken by our government during the Second World War.
I have doubts about that priority because three months have passed and we have not had any form of announcement in this House on when an apology will be forthcoming. Our Leader said quite articulately in his opening comments in this House that we favoured and all-party resolution that would apologize for those things that occurred during the Second World War. There is no question that a resolution of this kind would move through the House very rapidly. Why has it not come? Why is it being held up? Has the mechanism been swallowed up with time and consultation?
The second question about compensation is also worrisome. In my discussions with the Japanese Canadian community, the process is as equally important as the substance. Japanese Canadians would like some input into the whole process of determining what kind of compensation is appropriate. They would like a committee to look at the alternatives. They were promised by the current Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that a committee would look into the various features the compensation would take, to whom, and when.
On several occasions during Question Period I put questions to the Minister, but was unable to determine when this apology would be tabled in the House. Why has a committee not been formed? What kind of a committee was the Minister thinking about when he was out on the hustings and said that "We are committed to a committee"? What kind of membership will it have? Will there be members of the Japanese Canadian community on this committee? Will there be Parliamentarians from the three Parties on this committee? Will the committee travel across the country to touch base with the various elements?
This is not just a Japanese Canadian matter. The Minister knows full well there are various ethnocultural communities also supporting a resolution to this Japanese Canadian situation. The resolution of this issue is fundamental to their communities; their communities also in a small way have suffered similar experiences.
I mentioned that Japanese Canadians value the process as much as the substance. I have been quite worried about some of the discussions which have taken place. I have received reports that a chair of Japanese studies was being considered by the Minister as compensation. I asked the Minister about it in the House. He denied that it was a consideration. Only a few days later in an article in The Toronto Sun he was quoted as saying that that was being considered. My purpose is not to criticize or to make any value judgment on a chair of Japanese studies.
Another project came to my attention involving a several million dollar educational institute. I am not questioning whether that is right or wrong, appropriate or inappropriate. My concern is that those considerations are being percolated through the Department in isolation of Japanese Canadians, in isolation of this Parliament and in isolation of Canadians from coast to coast.
Also my concern is about the process. The Japanese Canadian community is very concerned that it be included in the process. To date I think it fair to say that Japanese Canadians have been somewhat frustrated about the process. They yearn for an announcement from the Minister or from the Government which would in fact keep the commitment they were given during the election.
I notice that I have 60 seconds or less to summarize this matter. I see that the Minister of State for Multiculturalism is present in the House. When can we expect an apology in terms of time frame? I am not playing politics because it is a sensitive issue, but after three months someone has to pick up the pieces and begin to work with them. When will an apology be forthcoming? Will a committee to study compensation be organized or established? My concern is that Japanese Canadians are being excluded from a process which largely deals with their community.

Mr. Speaker, I always listen to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) as he is knowledgeable in the area of multiculturalism. He comes from a very important part of the country which is immersed in multiculturalism; of course the City of Toronto.
The Hon. Member made two or three accusations which I will deal with before dealing with the Japanese Canadian issue. He indicated that we were bankrupt of ideas because nothing had really happened over the last three months. I am sure he knows that that is not the case.
My Department, my staff and myself have been moving in a number of areas. We are looking at a federal-provincial conference, of which the Hon. Member undoubtedly is aware. It will be the first one held in the area of multiculturalism. We have been dealing with racism through consultation with the chiefs of police in the country. We are looking at strengthening the appointment process which was sadly lacking after the last government was in power. We are moving to strengthen the
December 3, 1984

Department in some very significant ways. We are broadening the base of multiculturalism in terms of the areas we want to address and in terms of mainstreaming multiculturalism.
Of course we are addressing the Japanese Canadian issue, the whole question of compensation and apology. The basic reason the apology has not been forthcoming to this point in time is that there has been a lot of consultation. I have met with Japanese Canadians in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Toronto. We have discussed the matter at length. I am not exactly satisfied about the direction in which we should go, and certainly I will be looking for further consultation in the future. There is no question that there will be an acknowledgement in terms of what happened to that important community. Of course the Government will act. The question of compensation is important. It is being discussed at the present time. As I have previously said in the House, the Hon. Member will be one of the first persons to know our progress in this process. He may know before it is public. In fact, I hope he will know because I intend to talk with him and take him into my confidence on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to raise today concerns the rules and regulations of the Department of Transport which are destroying the second largest car rental company in Canada, Holiday Rent-A-Car. This company is fighting for its very survival because government regulations are preventing Holiday franchise holders from bidding for space at some of Canada's larger airports. This comes from a Government supposedly dedicated to fair and open competition and deregulation.
In a nutshell, this is the situation. Many Holiday franchise holders are being prevented from bidding for airport counter space on December 7 because previous Holiday franchise holders are in arrears to the Department. The Government regulations that make present Holiday franchise holders responsible for past debts is unfair. Certainly this principle does not exist in normal business practice or law. Let me give an example.
If 1 had a Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise and went into bankruptcy, owing money to the bank and property taxes, under this present Government regulation no one would be allowed to open a Kentucky Fried Chicken outlet until my debts were paid.
That is an unheard of business or legal principle. However, this is what is occurring at Canadian airports. The Minister must realize that this is unfair. In fact, when he was in opposition, he asked the former Minister of Transport to change the regulations.
In his reply to my question in the House, the Minister was incorrect when he stated "The Holiday Rent-A-Car organization is in considerable arrears". Holiday Rent-A-Car does not owe the Government-individual past franchise holders do.
Adjournment Debate
These are the people with whom the Government had a contract.
It is ludicrous that the Minister expects Holiday franchise holders in Vancouver, for example, to pay past arrears for people who now own the Budget franchise. The person who now owns the Budget franchise was the previous Holiday franchise holder in Vancouver. Under government regulations, the present franchise holder is expected to pay off those debts. That is ludicrous. I repeat, it is a principle that you do not find in normal business practice.
We are not asking the Government to write off these debts, but to collect them from the people that owe them. We are asking the Minister to stop holding the Holiday organization responsible and penalizing them to the point that they will go into bankruptcy. We plead with the Government to postpone the December 7 deadline and to refer this matter to a subcommittee of the Transport committee.
This is a complex issue. The best forum to deal with this is a subcommittee of the Transport committee which could call witnesses and hear testimony. A group of Members of Parliament from all sides of the House, hearing the evidence and considering the situation as it exists, will render a fair recommendation to the Minister and to this House. I therefore urge the Minister and the Government to consider these suggestions and proposals.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make the following observations to my friend, the Hon. Member foi Regina East (Mr. de Jong). Over the past two years, the Department of Transport has undertaken an extensive review of the 1979 airport vehicle rental concession policy to ensure its equitabili-ty and the provision of an open and competitive access to the airport market.
The policy, in particular the arrears provision, was seen by some to be too restrictive. This provision prevented any person or corporation in arrears to the Crown, or any person or corporation using the trade name or style of a company in arrears to the Crown from being awarded a vehicle rental contract at any Transport Canada airport until full payment of all arrears is received. The provision was established because of significant difficulties that arose as a result of the 1976 tender calls where some limited companies overbid and walked away from their airport debts.
In the 1979 tender call, the Department provided historical sales data that ensured prospective concessionaires would be aware of the dimensions of the market so that they could govern their bids accordingly. The Department, through these provisions, thus effectively served notice that it, like any other business, could not permit companies which were unable to pay their arrears to bid. Indeed, for Transport Canada not to insist on payment of rentals is unfair to competitive car rental companies and, in fact, I suppose, does a disservice to Canadian taxpayers.

December 3, 1984
Adjournment Debate
In order to provide Holiday and other companies in financial difficulties with some measure of relief, the policy was amended in October 1984, such that the prohibition against companies and trade names in arrears was applied on a site specific basis only. That is, a company in arrears at a particular airport may bid at that airport if all arrears are paid. In order to further facilitate entry into the airport market, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) further agreed that such rental arrears could be paid over the five-year term of the next contract.
The Minister of Transport tried on several occasions to reach a negotiated settlement with Holiday Rent-a-Car. These efforts have not been successful thus far. Nevertheless, individual Holiday operators not in arrears are most welcome to tender for new contracts at Transport Canada airports.
